# OmO **Your tool for real work. But it's an agent.** [English](README.md) | [简体中文](README.zh-cn.md) | [日本語](README.ja.md) | [Русский](README.ru.md) | [한국어](README.ko.md)
OmO is one `omo` command that turns your tokens into finished work: research across ten thousand sources, a deck people actually get, backends, frontends, code. It runs on senpi, our fork of [pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono), with everything below built in. ## Install ```bash curl -fsSL https://get.omo.dev/install.sh | bash omo ``` On Windows, in PowerShell: `irm https://get.omo.dev/install.ps1 | iex`. The script installs the native `omo` binary for your OS and CPU into `~/.local/bin`, checks it against the release checksums, and falls back to GitHub Releases when the mirror is unreachable. Add `-s -- beta` (or a version such as `-s -- 5.1.1`) after `bash` to pick another channel. Windows CMD, fixing your `PATH`, updating and uninstalling are covered at [omo.dev/docs/install](https://omo.dev/docs/install). Prefer a package manager? `bun add -g omo-ai` (or `npm i -g omo-ai`) installs the same OmO. The package is `omo-ai`; the unrelated `omo` package on npm is someone else's. Open your project, run `omo`, describe the job. That's the whole setup. In a session, `/thinking ` sets how hard the model thinks (`/thinking` alone opens a picker), `Shift+Tab` cycles through the levels, and `/efforts ` sets the reasoning effort directly on models with effort grades. To pick up earlier work, `/resume` (or `/sessions`) opens your past sessions; from the shell, `omo -c` continues the last one and `omo -r` opens the picker. `/help` lists everything else. Coming from the OpenCode edition or LazyCodex? Run `omo setup` once. It carries your provider keys, custom providers, MCP servers, skills and model picks across. `omo doctor` then shows which task categories your providers can run and what the old install left behind. The full walkthrough is [Migrating from OpenCode](docs/guide/migrating-from-opencode.md). To update, run the install line again (a package-manager install updates with `omo update`). `rm ~/.local/bin/omo` removes the binary install; `bun remove -g omo-ai` (or `npm uninstall -g omo-ai`) removes the package install. ## Why OmO **ultrawork.** Skip the study. If a task feels hard, add `ultrawork` (or `ulw`) to your prompt. The agent reads the codebase before touching a line, plans, proves each step before moving on, checks the result on the real surface, and stops when it's done. **Hundreds of agents, one keyword.** Type `mass ulw` and the whole job becomes a graph of agents: deep research over thousands of sources, a full machine-learning pipeline, a migration nobody wants to do. Each part runs on the model that fits it, in parallel, and gets checked before anything is called done. **Kibitzer. Your agent doesn't forget you, or your work.** Memory lives in a git repository of markdown files. A small, cheap model sits beside the expensive main agent, reads what you've done before, and nudges the main agent before it repeats a mistake. You stop re-explaining yourself. **Mix models without thinking about it.** Use the frontier models you love together with the cheap ones. Just sign in: `/login` covers Claude, ChatGPT, Kimi and GLM subscriptions. Every model ships with a system prompt tuned for it, so you never pick the wrong one. **High-quality skills, only the ones you need.** Your model is smart, but it still doesn't know a lot about solving real-world problems. OmO ships the missing knowledge as skills, browser use included, and loads only what the task needs. **Everything else is crafted.** Independent tool calls run together in one small program, so twenty reads are one round trip. Malformed tool arguments are repaired before they run. Waiting on a build or a deploy is a subscription, not polling. Long work keeps a record of what was checked, so a restarted session picks up where it stopped. Config, skills and prompts reload live. ## Configuration Opinionated defaults, adjustable if you insist. Your settings live in `~/.omo/omo.jsonc`, and a project can add its own `.omo/omo.jsonc`; the closest file wins. Every key is in the [configuration reference](docs/reference/configuration.md). ## Docs - [omo.dev/docs](https://omo.dev/docs) - [Migrating from OpenCode](docs/guide/migrating-from-opencode.md) - [Configuration reference](docs/reference/configuration.md) - [Features](docs/reference/features.md) - [Computer use](docs/guide/computer-use.md) (experimental) - [Ultrawork Manifesto](docs/manifesto.md) ## Reviews > "It made me cancel my Cursor subscription. Unbelievable things are happening in the open source community." - [Arthur Guiot](https://x.com/arthur_guiot/status/2008736347092382053?s=20) > "If Claude Code does in 7 days what a human does in 3 months, OmO does it in 1 hour."
- B, Quant Researcher > "You guys should pull this into core and recruit him. Seriously. It's really, really, really good."
- Henning Kilset ## Author's Note When I have to take the wheel back from an agent, that isn't teamwork. The system failed. OmO is built on that idea. You say what you want; the agent researches, plans, writes code you couldn't tell from a senior engineer's, verifies it, and keeps going until it's finished. It spends tokens when they buy real speed and routes the easy parts to cheap models. I'm this project's most obsessive user. Which model has the sharpest logic? Who writes the best prose? What did everyone else ship this week? OmO is where those answers land. Have a better way? PRs welcome. The goal is an agent you stop noticing. You flip the switch, the light turns on. The long version is the [Ultrawork Manifesto](docs/manifesto.md). No affiliation with any project or model mentioned. The Ultragoal and UltraQA ideas come from [oh-my-codex](https://github.com/Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-codex), reimplemented from concept for OmO. ## Loved by professionals at [Indent](https://indentcorp.com), makers of Spray (influencer marketing solution), vovushop (cross-border commerce platform) and vreview (AI commerce review marketing solution). [Google](https://google.com). [Microsoft](https://microsoft.com). [Vercel](https://vercel.com). [ELESTYLE](https://elestyle.jp), makers of elepay (multi-mobile payment gateway) and OneQR (mobile application SaaS for cashless solutions). [Deepgram](https://deepgram.com).

OmO

Your tool for real work. But it's an agent.

English | 简体中文 | 日本語 | Русский | 한국어

OmO is one omo command that turns your tokens into finished work: research across ten thousand sources, a deck people actually get, backends, frontends, code. It runs on senpi, our fork of pi, with everything below built in.

Install

curl -fsSL https://get.omo.dev/install.sh | bash
omo

On Windows, in PowerShell: irm https://get.omo.dev/install.ps1 | iex. The script installs the native omo binary for your OS and CPU into ~/.local/bin, checks it against the release checksums, and falls back to GitHub Releases when the mirror is unreachable. Add -s -- beta (or a version such as -s -- 5.1.1) after bash to pick another channel. Windows CMD, fixing your PATH, updating and uninstalling are covered at omo.dev/docs/install.

Prefer a package manager? bun add -g omo-ai (or npm i -g omo-ai) installs the same OmO. The package is omo-ai; the unrelated omo package on npm is someone else's.

Open your project, run omo, describe the job. That's the whole setup.

In a session, /thinking <level> sets how hard the model thinks (/thinking alone opens a picker), Shift+Tab cycles through the levels, and /efforts <level> sets the reasoning effort directly on models with effort grades. To pick up earlier work, /resume (or /sessions) opens your past sessions; from the shell, omo -c continues the last one and omo -r opens the picker. /help lists everything else.

Coming from the OpenCode edition or LazyCodex? Run omo setup once. It carries your provider keys, custom providers, MCP servers, skills and model picks across. omo doctor then shows which task categories your providers can run and what the old install left behind. The full walkthrough is Migrating from OpenCode.

To update, run the install line again (a package-manager install updates with omo update). rm ~/.local/bin/omo removes the binary install; bun remove -g omo-ai (or npm uninstall -g omo-ai) removes the package install.

Why OmO

ultrawork. Skip the study. If a task feels hard, add ultrawork (or ulw) to your prompt. The agent reads the codebase before touching a line, plans, proves each step before moving on, checks the result on the real surface, and stops when it's done.

Hundreds of agents, one keyword. Type mass ulw and the whole job becomes a graph of agents: deep research over thousands of sources, a full machine-learning pipeline, a migration nobody wants to do. Each part runs on the model that fits it, in parallel, and gets checked before anything is called done.

Kibitzer. Your agent doesn't forget you, or your work. Memory lives in a git repository of markdown files. A small, cheap model sits beside the expensive main agent, reads what you've done before, and nudges the main agent before it repeats a mistake. You stop re-explaining yourself.

Mix models without thinking about it. Use the frontier models you love together with the cheap ones. Just sign in: /login covers Claude, ChatGPT, Kimi and GLM subscriptions. Every model ships with a system prompt tuned for it, so you never pick the wrong one.

High-quality skills, only the ones you need. Your model is smart, but it still doesn't know a lot about solving real-world problems. OmO ships the missing knowledge as skills, browser use included, and loads only what the task needs.

Everything else is crafted. Independent tool calls run together in one small program, so twenty reads are one round trip. Malformed tool arguments are repaired before they run. Waiting on a build or a deploy is a subscription, not polling. Long work keeps a record of what was checked, so a restarted session picks up where it stopped. Config, skills and prompts reload live.

Configuration

Opinionated defaults, adjustable if you insist. Your settings live in ~/.omo/omo.jsonc, and a project can add its own .omo/omo.jsonc; the closest file wins. Every key is in the configuration reference.

Docs

  • omo.dev/docs
  • Migrating from OpenCode
  • Configuration reference
  • Features
  • Computer use (experimental)
  • Ultrawork Manifesto

Reviews

"If Claude Code does in 7 days what a human does in 3 months, OmO does it in 1 hour."
- B, Quant Researcher

Author's Note

When I have to take the wheel back from an agent, that isn't teamwork. The system failed. OmO is built on that idea. You say what you want; the agent researches, plans, writes code you couldn't tell from a senior engineer's, verifies it, and keeps going until it's finished. It spends tokens when they buy real speed and routes the easy parts to cheap models.

I'm this project's most obsessive user. Which model has the sharpest logic? Who writes the best prose? What did everyone else ship this week? OmO is where those answers land. Have a better way? PRs welcome.

The goal is an agent you stop noticing. You flip the switch, the light turns on. The long version is the Ultrawork Manifesto.

releases.name: v5.1.38
releases.body:
5.1.37 was tagged but its publish stopped on Linux (the release binaries outgrew their size budget), so its main packages never reached npm; everything listed for it ships in this release. ([#10566](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10566))

**Release binaries may be up to 182 MiB.** The per-platform size budget moves from 160 MiB to 182 MiB after measuring what grew: the Bun 1.4.3 runtime adds 9.5 MB to every binary and the senpi update about 1.25 MB, so linux-x64 reached 173.4 MB. Nothing was bundled by mistake. ([#10566](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10566))

5.1.36 was prepared but never published; everything listed for it ships in this release. ([#10552](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10552))

**The engine moves to senpi 2026.10.19: a hung extension handler no longer freezes a session, and queued input survives a crash.** An extension handler that never settles on a lifecycle event is named in the session after 60 s and released after 20 min, or at once on Esc or the turn deadline. Input queued with a client id is written to the session file before it is queued and delivered exactly once. The mouse wheel scrolls t

releases.name: v5.1.35
releases.body:
**The omo-senpi typecheck gives the same result wherever the checkout sits.** It used to pick up `@types/node` from folders above the checkout, so a stray older copy there failed the typecheck while CI passed on the same commit. omo-senpi now declares its own `@types/node` and `bun-types` and reads type packages only from its own `node_modules`. ([#10320](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/10320), [#10332](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10332))

**Memory items sync without losing concurrent edits, even from a stale device.** The sync item model captures a device's edits against the exact snapshot it saw, so a stale capture merges as a concurrent edit instead of silently dropping work or throwing; two captures from one device on one baseline lose nothing, multiline and quoted frontmatter values render as valid YAML on every replica, and path keys that would split one file into several (empty segments, trailing slashes, backslashes, drive letters) are rejected instead of canonicalized. Nothing syncs to a server yet. ([#10203](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10203))

**A `categories` entry named after an agent now gets a w

releases.name: v5.1.34
releases.body:
**`oracle`, `momus` and `plan-reviewer` fall back to Argon before the previous pro model.** In all three chains, Argon at high thinking (Google, Vertex or OpenCode) now sits directly ahead of the previous pro rung, which stays in place for Copilot and for engine pins that do not serve Argon yet. The GPT heads keep first place: on 8 consult and plan-review tasks graded blind, Argon beat the previous pro model in all 16 judgments but did not beat the current GPT heads on correctness, and its median answer took 57 s against 15 s. Telemetry now names the Qwen 3.7 Plus rung of `explore` and `librarian` instead of reporting it as `custom`. ([#10180](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/issues/10180), [#10263](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10263))

**`omo login`, `omo logout` and `omo whoami` are switched off until OmO accounts open.** OmO accounts aren't open to everyone yet. On every launcher (the npm `omo`, the compiled `omo` binary and the OpenCode-edition CLI), running `omo login`, `omo logout` or `omo whoami`, with any options including `--help`, prints "OmO accounts aren't available yet." and exits 1 without contacting the service or touching the O

releases.name: v5.1.33
releases.body: **omo runs on senpi 2026.10.13: a busy host gives memory back when its sessions end.** An RPC host serving many sessions used to keep the heap of every session it had run until it exited, so a long day of terminal-heavy work held its peak footprint; it now returns freed heap as sessions drop ([senpi#3240](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3240), [senpi#3221](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3221)). Tool calls through DeepSeek's official API, and gateways that forward to it, stop failing with `400 Invalid schema ... got 'type: null'`, because every tool schema now declares a root `type: "object"` ([senpi#3250](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3250)). The Claude subscription lane runs Claude Code 2.1.296 ([senpi#3258](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3258)), the model catalog is refreshed from the live providers ([senpi#3248](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3248)), large eval data cells no longer stall the shared host ([senpi#3206](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3206)), and RPC clients see a scheduled goal continuation and can run it now ([senpi#3208](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/senpi/pull/3208)). releases.name: v5.1.32
releases.body:
**5.1.32 is the release that 5.1.31 was meant to be: 5.1.31 never reached npm.** Two checks in the release pipeline stopped it before any package was published, one on the macOS Intel desktop engine and one on the Linux musl builds. omo itself did not change between the two, so every entry below is new to anyone upgrading from 5.1.30. The notarization check now waits for Apple's ticket to reach Gatekeeper, and the musl smoke no longer reports an exited host supervisor as a leak. ([#10081](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10081), [#10082](https://github.com/code-yeongyu/oh-my-openagent/pull/10082))

**omo runs on senpi 2026.10.12, and long sessions stop growing with every shell command.** A finished bash session used to keep its whole headless terminal screen (10,000 lines of scrollback plus replay history, about 20 MB for a 4,000-line output) until the 32-session limit evicted it, so a busy session or task host grew by that much per command; it now keeps only its final visible screen and its bounded output, and a live terminal's replay history is stored as flat strings instead of about 31 bytes per character. aiSummary.oneLiner: A powerful TUI harness and orchestrator for coding agents like Codex and OpenCode, optimized for complex codebases.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: oh-my-opencode (also known as LazyCodex) provides an advanced terminal user interface (TUI) and orchestration harness for AI coding agents. It is designed specifically to manage complex codebases by handling context effectively for models like Codex and OpenCode. The tool is currently undergoing a major refactor to support a multi-harness OS, allowing seamless switching between different agent backends. It emphasizes real-time, transparent building, with the maintainer actively streaming development using their own AI assistant. The project aims to provide the ultimate 'token-maximizing' environment for power users.
keyFeatures: Advanced terminal interface: Offers a rich, interactive TUI for managing agent interactions directly from the command line.
Multi-harness architecture: Supports seamless switching between different AI backends like OpenCode, Codex, and Pi.
Complex codebase management: Specifically engineered to handle large repositories by optimizing context windows and token usage.
Real-time public development: Maintained publicly using an AI assistant, ensuring transparency and rapid iteration.
Easy installation: Provides a simple npx command for quick deployment without complex local configuration.
Extensible orchestration: Acts as a central operating system for managing various specialized coding agents and skills.

useCases.title: Large repository navigation
useCases.description: Use the optimized context handling to ask questions and generate code within massive, intricate enterprise codebases.

useCases.title: Multi-model experimentation
useCases.description: Easily swap between Codex, OpenCode, and other agent harnesses to compare performance on specific coding tasks.

useCases.title: Terminal-based AI coding
useCases.description: Interact with powerful coding agents entirely within the terminal, maintaining workflow without switching to a graphical IDE.

useCases.title: Agent orchestration
useCases.description: Manage and coordinate multiple specialized AI assistants to tackle different aspects of a software project simultaneously.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Terminal power users, AI researchers, and developers managing complex codebases who need a robust, terminal-native agent harness. It is ideal for 'token-maxxers' who want granular control over how their AI assistants consume and generate code.
